doc.title: Emile Christian and Anthony Sbarbaro Interview, 1959-02-11

title: Belgian copyists and the 1919 London dance job
summary: The Belgians copy records note for note; Sbarbaro tells of playing a London club in 1919 against odd local bands.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: and they got a lot of these belgian boys over there they copy all the records you know they got some good bands over there just like the record is exactly note for note you write it out you know and they play it exactly and play good now they got some good musicians over there in belgium

you know what they had when we first played a dance over there in 1919 in a six-piece band and the six-piece band we went over there to play a uh after the theater went over to play a club job that's london this is london in a six-piece band they had two drummers that's how far they were advanced in music there so back fella had a bass drum that high every bit of past 36 inches and about that wide with one head on and there's two fellas playing drums and they couldn't understand how a trap was worked those days we had the overhead leading pedal which is out of and there's imagine what a band will sound like of course they always had trumpets in england they always had trombones and they always had you know legit clarinism but the average band that we had a buck up against playing in a place where we at was two banjos piano and a drum they all had colored drummers ahead of the head of it and that'll be a jazz band they thought that'd be a colored drummer and what they would sound like you know two bands then later on they were going to go to town and bring something to kill us because we were getting too much of their money they brought a band that hadn't even seen each other on the boat i know all the boys i still see them in new york some of them are still living the band consisted of a fiddle a banjo a trombone piano and drums i still see the fiddle player romana i don't know where the trombone i still see the banjo banjo wallace and i still steal the dave fuller the piano player and eddie the drummer stood over there and he married a rich girl david
dead who's dave david wallace banjo i don't know who's but i don't see him i already died but uh you

can imagine what a fiddle banjo and trombone piano drum band sounded like so this boss he almost flipped these lids you know it cost him all that money you know i remember it cost us about 250 dollars one you know one way in those days and after playing all that money then uh well we had him against the wall he had to do what we said from then on but the place that we opened after we got finished working for all of them that pali the dance is still a big thing in europe still a very big thing i walked into a in the commodore music shop which jack crystal i do you know a lot of that stuff on second animal front and they got a very bad man uh overseeing their father about 70 years old and you pick up a book you got to buy it so i felt embarrassed because the book was only a quarter i took the book and i opened it up and the middle page of this big magazine you know this is a second hand magazine it will be old but there's a whole thing with the original dixieland picture smacked over there he didn't know he was doing me a big favor if he saw me look at that he'd have charged me a dollar a quarter
